opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that better models change drug discovery less by producing a magic molecule and more by changing where the bottlenecks sit.

Today, most of the cost and time goes into a long chain of guess, make, test, repeat. You pick a target and hypothesize that hitting it will help a disease. Then you screen or design molecules, synthesize them, run assays, and find out most of them don't work, or they work but are toxic, or they don't get where they need to go in the body. Then you iterate, often for years, and roughly ninety percent of what enters clinical trials still fails.

Better models can attack that at a few points.

The first is target selection. A lot of clinical failures aren't chemistry failures. The biology hypothesis was just wrong. Models trained on genetics, single-cell data, perturbation screens, and patient outcomes can help you ask, before you've spent a dollar on chemistry, whether modulating a target is actually likely to change the disease in humans. If you improve that hit rate even modestly, it compounds through the whole pipeline.

The second is design. Structure prediction and generative models for proteins and small molecules let you explore chemical space much more broadly than a medicinal chemist's intuition alone. More importantly, you can optimize several properties at once: potency, selectivity, solubility, metabolic stability, predicted toxicity. You stop having to fix one problem and accidentally create another.

The third, which I think is underrated, is closing the loop with the lab. The models are only as good as the data, and public data is noisy and biased toward things people already found interesting. The teams I find most exciting pair models with automated, high-throughput experiments, so the model proposes, the lab tests, and the results feed straight back in. That's where you get real compounding, because you generate exactly the data the model is uncertain about instead of whatever happens to exist.

And then there's the clinical side: better patient stratification, predicting who will respond, designing smarter trials. That's less glamorous, but it's where a huge share of the money goes.

The caveat I'd add is that biology is still the hard part. A model can tell you a molecule binds beautifully, and it can still fail because the disease mechanism was misunderstood or because the human body is just more complicated than any assay. So I don't think AI replaces wet labs or clinical trials anytime soon. What it can realistically do is make each experiment more informative and each failure cheaper and earlier. If you fail fast in silico instead of slowly in phase two, that alone changes the economics of the whole industry.

r001.rationale: The response describes the drug-development chain as “guess, make, test, repeat” and proposes a model–lab feedback loop in which model suggestions are tested and results feed back in.

r002.rationale: It discusses better models changing bottlenecks, but does not say drug-discovery products must operate at higher levels of abstraction as models improve.

r003.rationale: It mentions structure prediction, generative design, and lab feedback, but does not propose composing structure-prediction, binding, and molecular-design models to participate in a broader scientific discovery loop.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that better models don't change drug discovery by replacing the wet lab, they change it by changing where the bottleneck sits.

Right now the expensive part isn't generating candidate molecules. We can generate millions of them. The expensive part is deciding which ten to actually synthesize and test, because every one of those costs weeks and real money, and most of them fail for reasons that had nothing to do with the thing you designed them for. Off-target toxicity, poor solubility, it doesn't get absorbed, whatever. So the game is really about how many wrong guesses you can afford before you run out of budget.

Where models help is in compressing that loop. If a model can tell you with reasonable confidence that a compound is going to have a liver toxicity problem before you ever make it, you've just saved a cycle. Do that across binding, ADME properties, synthesizability, and suddenly your hit rate in the lab goes from maybe one in a hundred to one in ten. That's not a small efficiency gain, that's a different kind of program.

The second thing, and I think this is underrated, is that the newer models are much better at reading. A huge amount of what we know about biology is locked up in papers, patents, internal lab notebooks, assay results that someone ran in 2014 and nobody looked at again. A model that can actually synthesize across all of that and say, hey, this target you're excited about, there's a failed program from a decade ago that hit the same mechanism and here's why it died, that's enormously valuable. Most of the industry's institutional memory is just lost.

Where I'd push back on the hype is the idea that we're close to a model that just designs a drug end to end. Biology is adversarial in a way that chemistry isn't. The body pushes back. Clinical trials fail for reasons we don't understand, and no amount of in silico work fixes the fact that you eventually have to put the molecule in a person. So I see the models as making the humans dramatically faster at the early stages, and maybe making them a bit wiser about which bets to take, rather than removing them from the picture.

r001.rationale: The response says models can compress the drug-discovery loop and improve candidate selection, but does not describe changing a sequence of gated stages into an iterative loop.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that drug-discovery products need to operate at higher levels of abstraction as models improve.

r003.rationale: It mentions models for binding and other properties, but does not propose composing structure prediction, binding, and molecular-design models to join a broader scientific discovery loop.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest shift is that better models can help us choose better experiments. Drug discovery involves searching an enormous space of possible molecules with limited time and resources. If a model can help predict which candidates are worth testing—and where those predictions are uncertain—you can make that search much more efficient.

But generating a promising molecule is only part of the problem. It also has to reach the right tissue, have the intended effect, and be safe. So the exciting possibility is a tighter loop: make a prediction, test it in the lab, learn from the result, and use that evidence to choose the next experiment. Better models could help us learn more from each experiment, even when it fails.

That doesn’t eliminate the need for experimental or clinical validation. It could mean we arrive at those stages with stronger candidates and a better understanding of why they might work.

r001.rationale: The response describes models predicting candidates, followed by lab testing and learning from results to choose the next experiment—a drug discovery process framed as an iterative loop.

r002.rationale: The response does not argue that drug-discovery products need to operate at higher levels of abstraction as models improve.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose composing structure-prediction, binding, and molecular-design models to participate in a broader scientific discovery loop.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is making the loop between a hypothesis and an experiment much faster. In drug discovery, you’re searching an enormous space of possible molecules, and you have several constraints at once: does it affect the biology you care about, can you get it to the right tissue, is it safe, can you manufacture it?

Better models could help you navigate those tradeoffs and choose more informative experiments. Instead of just asking, “Which molecule looks most promising?” you can ask, “What should we test next to reduce our uncertainty?” Then you take those results and feed them back into the model.

But the key is that the predictions still have to survive contact with biology. Generating a molecule is very different from demonstrating that it’s a useful drug. So I’d look for progress in how reliably these systems help experimental teams learn—and ultimately whether that leads to better treatments.
